learningObjective: Distinguish end-to-end latency from microbenchmark latency and identify when a microbenchmark speedup does not translate to end-to-end speedup.
stem: A team reports a 4.7× speedup on a fused LayerNorm+bias microbenchmark and concludes the end-to-end model inference will speed up by 4.7×. Which critique is most accurate?

options.text: The 4.7× is correct because kernel-level speedups compose multiplicatively into end-to-end speedup as long as at least one op is sped up; the only limit is the Amdahl fraction of the sped-up op, and LayerNorm is a mainstream op so its fraction is always high.

The microbenchmark speedup is an underestimate: fusing LayerNorm with adjacent bias unlocks cache reuse in following ops as well, so the end-to-end speedup is typically 2-3× larger than the microbenchmark number.

Since the microbenchmark speedup is 4.7×, the end-to-end speedup will be exactly 4.7× minus the launch-overhead constant of 5 µs times the number of layers; for typical 32-layer models this gives ≈ 4.6× end-to-end.

Kernel and end-to-end speedups can differ substantially: only the fraction of end-to-end time actually spent in that kernel is affected by the microbenchmark improvement (Amdahl's law). If LayerNorm is 5% of end-to-end time, a 4.7× kernel speedup translates into at most ≈ 4% end-to-end improvement, not 4.7×.

explanation: End-to-end speedup follows Amdahl's law: if the optimized op consumes fraction f of end-to-end time and is sped up by k, the end-to-end speedup is at most 1 / ((1-f) + f/k). For a small f the achievable end-to-end speedup is bounded well below k. Options A, B, C fabricate compositional or additive relationships that don't hold.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: kernel and end-to-end speedups do not compose multiplicatively without weighting by time fraction.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: cross-op cache effects exist but typically shrink, not amplify, the reported gain in end-to-end.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: no such fixed launch-overhead subtraction rule.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: Amdahl's law bounds the end-to-end improvement.

assumptions: The microbenchmark measures the kernel in isolation, not with surrounding realistic context.
The end-to-end pipeline includes many other kernels.
nonImplications: Does not imply LayerNorm optimization is useless; even a small end-to-end gain matters at scale.
Does not imply Amdahl is the only concern; batch effects and cross-op memory traffic can also cause divergence.

performanceClaim.scope: Kernel-level microbenchmark speedup vs end-to-end speedup under Amdahl's law
